title: Where to Go From Here
sub: A map of what you can do now, what to learn next, and a routine that gets you there
goals: List the skills you now have and the chapter where each one lives
Choose one next track (security, Linux, packet crafting, automation, Python depth or web development) and a first project for it
Keep a weekly practice routine that fits around other things
Read primary documentation (man pages, PEPs, RFCs) instead of searching for summaries
Practice offensive skills only on systems built or authorized for it

blocks.text: You started with a terminal prompt and a question about what a packet is. You now read `tcpdump` output, resolve names by hand, write zsh scripts, parse logs with `awk`, talk to servers in Python, and ship a tested package. This chapter does not teach anything new. It shows where each road leads, what to read, where to practice safely, and how to keep going without a schedule that depends on motivation.
What you can do now

Read this table once, quickly, and mark the rows you could not do without looking something up. Those rows are your first review list. Looking things up is normal; the question is whether you know what to look up.

blocks.text: Create `~/lab/review.txt` and write one line per weak row, with a command to rehearse. For example: `dig +trace example.com   # explain each referral`. Next week's practice sessions come from this file. Keep it in git.
What "intermediate" means now

You are an intermediate practitioner when you can solve a problem you have not seen before by combining tools, and you recover from failures by reading the error and checking one thing at a time. That is a method, not a body of facts. The facts you still lack are all things you can look up in minutes. The method is what you built over these chapters:

items.text: State the symptom exactly (which command, which message, which host).
Split the system into layers or stages and test the middle ([Troubleshooting](#troubleshoot)).
Change one thing, observe, and write down the result.
Read the primary source for the thing that surprised you.

blocks.text: The next skill level adds **depth in one direction** and **breadth by building projects that need you to learn something new**. Pick a direction below. You do not need all of them.
Six tracks
Track 1: Network security fundamentals
Security work starts with an accurate model of what a system does, which is what you have been building. Add these concepts, in this order:

items.text: **Threat modelling**: what is valuable, who could attack it, how. Draw your home network and mark where an attacker could be: the Wi-Fi, a malicious web page, a compromised IoT device, a stolen laptop.

**Cryptography as a user**: hashing versus encryption versus signing, why passwords are stored with slow salted hashes (`argon2`, `bcrypt`, `scrypt`), what TLS certificates prove. Use `openssl` and `hashlib` to see each one.
**The web attack classes**: injection, broken authentication, cross-site scripting, request forgery. The OWASP Top 10 lists them with examples.

**Network defence**: segmentation (VLANs), firewalls (`pf` on macOS, `nftables` on Linux), logs and what normal looks like. A scan, a brute-force attempt and a DNS tunnel all show up in logs you already know how to analyse.
**Reconnaissance tools** you already use responsibly: `nmap`, `dig`, `curl`, Wireshark. Add `nmap` NSE scripts in the safe categories, only on your own lab.

blocks.text: Testing a system without the owner's permission is illegal in most countries, whatever your intention, and "I was only looking" is not a defence. Practice on your own equipment, on virtual machines you built, and on platforms made for it (listed below). A written scope that names hosts, dates and allowed actions is what separates a penetration test from an intrusion.

A first project: write `loginwatch.py` that tails an `auth.log` or `ssh` log from a lab Linux VM, counts failed logins per source IP in a sliding window, and prints a ban list in `pf` or `nftables` syntax without applying it. It reuses `Counter`, `re`, file following and time windows from this book.
Track 2: Linux administration

Most servers you will ever meet run Linux. You already know most of the shell. What changes is the system layer. Install Debian or Ubuntu in a VM (UTM, VMware Fusion or VirtualBox) or on a Raspberry Pi, and rehearse with the table below, which maps the macOS commands you know to their Linux counterparts.

The Linux topics that repay study: users, groups and `sudoers`; systemd units and timers (the equivalent of `launchd`); `journalctl`; `cron`; the filesystem hierarchy standard (`/etc`, `/var/log`, `/srv`); disk and LVM basics; SSH hardening ([SSH](#ssh) has the checklist); and a firewall with a default-deny inbound policy. A first project: build a small server VM that runs your `api_server.py` as a systemd service behind a firewall that allows only SSH and port 8080, and check from your Mac with `portscan.py` (your own VM, so allowed) that nothing else is open.
Track 3: Packet crafting with scapy
In [Python networking](#py-net) you built packets from bytes with `struct`. `scapy` does the same with layered objects, and it can also dissect captures. The shape of the API is small:

items.text: `IP(dst="192.168.1.1") / ICMP()` stacks layers with `/`.
`sr1(pkt, timeout=2)` sends one packet and returns the first answer, `srp` does the same at layer 2 (needed for ARP scans on your LAN).
`sniff(filter="icmp", count=5, prn=lambda p: p.summary())` captures with a BPF filter, exactly like `tcpdump`.
`rdpcap("file.pcap")` reads a capture you made earlier, and `wrpcap` writes one.

blocks.name: scapy sniff
blocks.sum: Capture packets from Python and print or process them, using BPF filters like tcpdump.

how.text: `sniff` opens the interface through libpcap, applies the kernel-level BPF `filter` string, and calls `prn(packet)` for every match. Packets arrive as layered objects, so `p[IP].src` and `p[TCP].dport` replace manual `struct` unpacking. Capturing needs root. Install scapy in a venv and call that venv's interpreter with `sudo`, because plain `sudo python3` may use a different Python.

examples.desc: Print a one-line summary of three ICMP packets on loopback (run `ping -c 3 127.0.0.1` in another tab)
examples.code: sudo .venv/bin/python -c 'from scapy.all import sniff; sniff(iface="lo0", filter="icmp", count=3, prn=lambda p: print(p.summary()))'

gotchas: On macOS the loopback interface is `lo0`. Check names with `ifconfig -l`. If nothing prints, you are capturing on the wrong interface or the filter excludes your traffic.

blocks.text: A first project: `arpscan.py` that sends an ARP request to every address of your own /24 with `srp(Ether(dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff")/ARP(pdst="192.168.1.0/24"), timeout=2)`, and prints IP, MAC and vendor for each answer. Compare its result with `arp -a` and your `lan-inventory`. Only run it on your own network.

`nmap --script` for scripted service checks, `hping3` and `nping` for hand-built probes, `Wireshark` Lua dissectors, and the Python `dpkt` library for fast offline parsing of large captures. Learn scapy first because its Python interface fits what you already know.
Track 4: Automation
Automation turns your scripts into things that run without you.

items.text: **Scheduling**: `launchd` on macOS and `systemd` timers or `cron` on Linux ([Scripting](#scripting)). A job needs a log file, a lock so two runs cannot overlap, and a notification when it fails.
**Configuration as code**: describe the state you want and let a tool converge on it. Ansible does this over SSH with YAML playbooks and needs nothing installed on the target.

**Repeatable environments**: pin dependencies (`pip freeze`, or a lock file from `uv`), put project setup in a `Makefile` or `justfile`, and use containers when a program must run the same everywhere.
**Continuous integration**: run `pytest` on every push, using GitHub Actions or any CI service. Your `netkit` tests need no network, so they are ideal for this.
**APIs**: most services expose REST or GraphQL. You know HTTP, so reading an API reference is mostly learning what the endpoints are called. Use `requests` and `curl | jq` side by side.

blocks.text: A first project: take `netcheck.zsh` or `netkit ping`, run it from `launchd` every five minutes, append JSON lines to a log, and write a 20-line script that mails or notifies you when three consecutive checks fail.
Track 5: Python depth and other languages

Python skills worth adding, in value order: `pytest` depth (fixtures, parametrization, mocking), type hints with `mypy` or `pyright`, packaging and publishing, `asyncio` for network services, SQL with `sqlite3` then PostgreSQL, and profiling (`cProfile`, `timeit`). Read the standard library source for modules you use daily; it is clear, readable Python.

Learn a second language to see what Python hides. **Go** is the usual next step for network tools: static binaries, goroutines, a standard library with a full HTTP server and TLS. **Rust** teaches ownership and memory safety, and is used in security tooling and systems work. **C** is worth a month if you want to understand sockets, memory and the kernel interface that Python wraps. A first project in any of them: re-implement `portscan.py` and compare the speed and the amount of code.
Track 6: Web development depth
You can now build pages, write JavaScript, debug in DevTools and serve an API with Node.js. The next layers, in value order:

items.text: **TypeScript**: JavaScript with static types; catches whole classes of bugs before you run the code and makes larger front ends manageable. Start by adding `// @ts-check` to a JavaScript file, then move one module to `.ts`.
**Accessibility and semantics in practice**: test your dashboard with VoiceOver (⌘F5 on a Mac) and the keyboard only. Fix what you find.

**A front-end framework, after the basics feel easy**: React, Vue or Svelte all build on the DOM, events, modules and `fetch` you learned. Read their official tutorials; you will recognise the problems they solve (re-rendering lists, state, components).
**Databases behind your API**: SQLite from Node (`node:sqlite` in recent Node versions, or a package), then PostgreSQL.

**Web security**: the OWASP Top 10, cookies (`HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite`), Content Security Policy, authentication with sessions vs tokens. Practise on deliberately vulnerable apps such as OWASP Juice Shop, run locally.
**Deployment**: a reverse proxy (Caddy or nginx) with TLS on a Pi in your lab, a process manager, logs. The networking part of this book is exactly what you need to debug it.

blocks.text: Primary documentation: MDN Web Docs (developer.mozilla.org) for HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Web APIs; the WHATWG HTML and DOM standards when MDN is not enough; nodejs.org/api for Node; web.dev for performance and accessibility guidance.
A weekly routine that survives a busy week
Consistency beats intensity. This schedule takes about five hours a week and degrades gracefully: if you only have one session, do the first.

head: Session
Length
What
rows: Take three lines from `review.txt`. Without notes, run the command or write the snippet, then check. Update the file.
Work on the current project. End every session with a commit and a one-line note on what to do next.
One man page or RFC section, or one chapter of a book. Write three sentences of summary in your own words.
In a VM or on `localhost`, break a service on purpose (wrong config, full disk, blocked port), then diagnose it only with the tools from the troubleshooting method.
One wargame level, CTF challenge or Advent of Code puzzle (links below).

blocks.text: Keep a **lab notebook**: a plain text or Markdown file where each entry has the date, the question, the commands you ran, what happened and what you learned. Mistakes written down are the cheapest learning there is, and in a month the notebook is your own searchable reference, better than any cheat sheet you did not write.
Reading documentation
Learning to read primary sources is the largest single multiplier. Order your attention like this:

items.text: `command --help` and `man command`. In a man page, search with `/` and a keyword, jump with `n` and `N`, quit with `q`. Read EXAMPLES first and FLAGS second.
`tldr`, a community collection of short, practical examples: `brew install tldr`, then `tldr tar`. Use it to remember, not to learn; follow up in the man page.

Python: `help(obj)`, `python3 -m pydoc name`, and the documentation at docs.python.org. **PEPs** (Python Enhancement Proposals) explain why the language is the way it is: PEP 8 (style), PEP 20 (the Zen of Python), PEP 257 (docstrings), PEP 484 (type hints), PEP 668 (the externally-managed environment error you met), PEP 3156 (asyncio's design).
**RFCs** are the protocols themselves. They are less hard to read than their reputation. Start with the ones that match what you did in this book:

head: Topic
RFC
Why read it
rows: Echo, TTL exceeded, unreachable: what `ping` and `traceroute` use
Three pages; the shortest useful RFC
The current specification (it replaced RFC 793); the state machine behind `netstat`
Long, but the handshake overview is readable
The notation and the address types

blocks.text: Read an RFC with a capture beside it. Open the capture of one HTTP request and match each field to a line in the document. That pairing is how the formats stay in memory.
Places to practice

Every site below provides systems you are **allowed** to attack, inside their rules. Do not extend the techniques to anything else. Read the terms of each platform, stay inside the stated scope, and never test a shared hosting service, a school or a workplace network "just to see". Your own VMs are always in scope.

blocks.text: A home lab is the best resource, and it is cheap: a Raspberry Pi or an old laptop with Linux, a managed switch that supports VLANs, and your Mac. Segment a "lab" network from your normal one, run the services you wrote, and attack and defend them.
Certifications as signposts

Certifications are optional. They help when an employer filters on them, and they give a syllabus to follow when you want one. They do not replace a portfolio of working projects. A list of reasonable signposts, from the base up:

blocks.text: Check each vendor's current objectives and exam format before you buy a course, because they are revised every few years. Use the objectives list as a checklist against your own notebook: for each line, can you demonstrate it on a command line?
Reading list
One line each on why it earns its place. Pick two and finish them before buying more.

items.text: **Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach** (Kurose and Ross). The standard university text, organized from applications down; pairs well with what you did hands-on.
**TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1** (W. Richard Stevens, second edition with Kevin Fall). The protocols explained with real packet traces, which you can now reproduce yourself.
**The Linux Command Line** (William Shotts). Free online; deeper on the shell and scripting than most guides.
**Automate the Boring Stuff with Python** (Al Sweigart). Free online; practical file, web and automation recipes.
**Fluent Python** (Luciano Ramalho). The best book for understanding why Python behaves as it does: data model, iterators, decorators, concurrency.
**Black Hat Python** (Justin Seitz and Tim Arnold). Networking and packet manipulation in Python, written for security work; use it only on authorized systems.
**Practical Packet Analysis** (Chris Sanders). Wireshark methods on real problems.
**UNIX and Linux System Administration Handbook** (Nemeth et al.). The reference for running Linux systems.
**Serious Cryptography** (Jean-Philippe Aumasson). Cryptography for engineers, without needing advanced mathematics.
**The Rust Programming Language** and **The Go Programming Language** (Donovan and Kernighan). Official, readable introductions to the two usual next languages.
**Hacking: The Art of Exploitation** (Jon Erickson). C, memory, and networking for security-minded readers; the exploitation chapters need a lab setup.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Pick a track and write a one-page plan

task.text: Choose one of the six tracks. Write, in `~/lab/plan.md`: the track, the first project from this chapter, three concrete milestones with dates inside the next 30 days, and the first command you will type. Commit it.

blocks.solution: A plan is complete when each milestone is observable: "port scanner passes tests and runs against the lab VM by the 14th" works, "learn more about security" does not. The first command might be `git init ~/lab/track1 && cd ~/lab/track1` or `limactl start` for a VM.

why.text: Observable milestones tell you on a given date whether you are on schedule, and a typed first command removes the activation cost of starting.

blocks.title: Read RFC 792 against a capture

task.text: Run `ping -c 1 127.0.0.1` while `sudo tcpdump -i lo0 -nn -vv -c 2 icmp` runs in another tab. Open RFC 792 (the ICMP specification) and find the Echo Message type and code values. Match them to the `ICMP echo request` and `echo reply` lines in the capture.

hints: Echo request is type 8 and echo reply is type 0, both with code 0.
blocks.solution:
sudo tcpdump -i lo0 -nn -vv -c 2 icmp
# second tab:
ping -c 1 127.0.0.1

why.text: Reading a specification beside a trace is the quickest way to learn a protocol. The numbers in the RFC and the words tcpdump prints are the same facts.

blocks.title: Port a command to Linux

task.text: Take your `netcheck.zsh` or one `netkit` function and list every line that would behave differently on Debian Linux. Use the mapping table in Track 2 as a guide. Write the replacement for each.

blocks.solution: Common differences are `ping -W` (milliseconds on macOS, seconds on Linux), `ifconfig` versus `ip addr`, `sed -i ''` versus `sed -i`, `date -v-1d` versus `date -d yesterday`, `route -n get default` versus `ip route show default`, and the `ping` summary text (`packets received` versus `received`).

why.text: Portability is a skill you build by finding differences, and the habit pays off when a script that worked on your Mac fails on a server.

blocks.title: Build a review file

task.text: Create `~/lab/review.txt` with ten lines, each a command or snippet from this book that you want to be able to produce from memory. Write a zsh function `quiz` that prints one random line using `sort -R | head -1`, then prompts you to type it, and prints the line after you press Return.

hints: `read -r` waits for input; `sort -R` shuffles lines on macOS.
blocks.solution:
quiz() {
  local line
  line=$(sort -R ~/lab/review.txt | head -1)
  print -r -- "Type from memory, then press Return to reveal:"
  read -r
  print -r -- "$line"
}

why.text: Spaced self-testing works better than rereading. A tiny tool you wrote yourself makes it a habit.

blocks.verify: zsh -n <(print -r -- 'quiz() { local line; line=$(sort -R ~/lab/review.txt | head -1); read -r; print -r -- "$line"; }') && echo OK

questions.q: Which RFC is the current TCP specification?
questions.why: RFC 9293 (2022) consolidated and replaced RFC 793, the original 1981 specification.

questions.q: You want to practice scanning and exploitation skills. Which is acceptable?

options.text: Your neighbour's router, since it uses default credentials
A website that looks poorly maintained
A virtual machine you built, or a platform that explicitly authorizes testing

questions.why: Written permission from the owner is what makes testing legal. Your own VMs and purpose-built platforms provide it.

questions.q: On macOS, `ping -W 1000` waits one second. What does the equivalent on Linux look like?
questions.why: macOS takes milliseconds for `-W`; Linux takes seconds. This difference breaks scripts that are moved between the systems.

questions.q: Which tool is the Linux counterpart of `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` for listing listening TCP sockets?
questions.why: `ss` replaced `netstat` on modern Linux; `-t` TCP, `-l` listening, `-n` numeric, `-p` process.

questions.q: Which habit best makes your skills last?

options.text: Short, regular sessions that include building something, testing recall and reading primary sources

questions.why: Spaced practice, retrieval and building new things move knowledge into long-term memory. Flags are cheap to look up.

blocks.text: "I can now..." checklist
Tick these off for real. For each, run the command, do not just recognize it.

items.text: [ ] I can explain what happens between typing a URL and the page appearing, naming each protocol and the tool I would use to observe it.
[ ] I can compute network, broadcast and usable range for any IPv4 CIDR by hand and confirm it with `ipaddress`.
[ ] I can write a five-stage pipeline that answers a question about a log file.
[ ] I can write a zsh script with functions, arguments, `set` safety options, and meaningful exit codes.
[ ] I can diagnose "the internet is broken" layer by layer with specific commands and expected outputs.
[ ] I can read a `tcpdump` line and a Wireshark TCP stream.
[ ] I can open an SSH tunnel and explain which end each of `-L`, `-R` and `-D` listens on.
[ ] I can write a Python TCP client and server and explain why TCP needs message framing.
[ ] I can parse an IPv4 header from hex with `struct`.
[ ] I can write tests for a function and for a command-line tool, and I run them before I commit.
[ ] I can package a project so another person can install it with one command.
[ ] I know which systems I may test, and I have never scanned one I may not.

blocks.text: If most boxes are ticked, you have the foundation. The remaining work is repetition in a direction you care about. Pick a track, write the plan, type the first command.
Glossary
Back to the start: [Welcome](#welcome), or open the [Command Atlas](#cheats) to look up any command from this book.

terms.def: A structured description of what you protect, who might attack it and how
A hosted set of security puzzles designed to be attacked legally
Capture the flag: a competition or practice set where you solve security challenges to find hidden strings
A virtual LAN: a switch feature that splits one physical network into separate broadcast domains
The service manager on most Linux systems, the counterpart of launchd
Python Enhancement Proposal: a design document describing a change or convention in Python
Request for Comments: the numbered documents that specify Internet protocols
Berkeley Packet Filter: the kernel mechanism and expression syntax for selecting packets
A dated log of questions, commands, results and conclusions kept while learning
